The Implementation of Standardized Testing in Schools: A Detriment to Student Success. 

The debate over the effectiveness of standardized testing in schools has been ongoing for years. While proponents argue that these tests provide an objective measure of student knowledge, I firmly believe that they have a detrimental impact on the educational system. Standardized tests, such as the SAT and ACT, have become a staple in many schools, with the results often being used to determine college admissions and future career prospects.

However, these tests only measure a narrow range of skills, primarily focusing on math and reading comprehension. This creates a limited view of a student's abilities, neglecting important aspects such as creativity, critical thinking, and problem-solving. By placing such a heavy emphasis on standardized testing, schools are inadvertently encouraging a culture of rote memorization, where students are more focused on achieving a high test score than genuinely learning and understanding the material.

Furthermore, standardized testing can be a significant source of stress and anxiety for students. The pressure to perform well on these tests can be overwhelming, leading to a range of negative effects on mental health and well-being. This is particularly concerning, as students are already faced with numerous academic and social pressures. By removing standardized testing from the equation, schools can help alleviate some of this stress and create a more supportive and inclusive learning environment.

In addition, standardized testing can be biased towards certain demographics, often favoring students from affluent backgrounds who have had greater access to test preparation resources. This can result in a disproportionate number of students from lower-income families being unfairly disadvantaged, further exacerbating existing social and economic inequalities. By relying on standardized testing as a primary assessment tool, schools are perpetuating a system that is inherently unfair and unjust.

Rather than relying on standardized testing, schools should focus on implementing more holistic and comprehensive assessment methods. This could include project-based evaluations, peer review, and self-assessment, which would provide a more nuanced and accurate picture of a student's abilities and potential. By adopting this approach, schools can create a more inclusive and supportive learning environment, where students are encouraged to take risks, explore their interests, and develop a genuine love of learning.

In conclusion, while standardized testing may have been implemented with the intention of promoting accountability and improving academic standards, it has ultimately had a negative impact on the educational system. By recognizing the limitations and biases of standardized testing, schools can take a crucial step towards creating a more equitable and effective learning environment, where students are able to thrive and reach their full potential. It is time for educators and policymakers to rethink their approach to assessment and adopt a more comprehensive and inclusive approach to evaluating student success.

The implementation of universal basic income (UBI) has been a topic of debate in recent years. As someone who is passionate about social welfare and economic equality, I firmly believe that UBI is a necessary step towards creating a more just and equitable society. The concept of UBI is simple: every citizen receives a regular, unconditional sum of money from the government to cover their basic needs. This amount would be enough to provide a decent standard of living, allowing people to meet their fundamental needs such as food, shelter, and healthcare.

One of the primary arguments against UBI is that it would be too expensive to implement and maintain. However, I would argue that the benefits of UBI far outweigh the costs. For one, UBI would help to reduce poverty and income inequality, which are two of the most pressing issues facing our society today. By providing a safety net for all citizens, UBI would ensure that everyone has access to the resources they need to thrive, regardless of their background or circumstances.

Another argument against UBI is that it would reduce the incentive for people to work. However, this argument is based on a flawed assumption that people only work for financial gain. In reality, many people work because they are passionate about their jobs, or because they want to contribute to society. UBI would actually enable people to pursue their passions and interests, rather than just taking any job for the sake of a paycheck. Additionally, UBI would give people the financial security to start their own businesses, or to pursue entrepreneurial ventures, which could lead to innovation and economic growth.

Furthermore, UBI would have numerous positive effects on mental and physical health. Financial stress is a major contributor to anxiety and depression, and UBI would help to alleviate this stress by providing a sense of security and stability. It would also enable people to access healthcare services and healthy food, which would lead to improved physical health outcomes. In fact, a study in Finland found that UBI recipients experienced improved well-being, life satisfaction, and trust in institutions.

In conclusion, I strongly believe that UBI is a necessary step towards creating a more just and equitable society. While there are concerns about the cost and potential impact on work incentives, I believe that the benefits of UBI far outweigh the drawbacks. By providing a safety net for all citizens, UBI would help to reduce poverty and income inequality, enable people to pursue their passions and interests, and improve mental and physical health outcomes. It is time for us to rethink our social welfare systems and consider the implementation of UBI as a key component of a more equitable and just society.

The impact of social media on society has been a topic of debate in recent years. While some argue that social media has numerous benefits, such as connecting people worldwide and providing a platform for self-expression, others claim that it has a multitude of negative effects. In this essay, I will argue that the negative effects of social media far outweigh its benefits.

First and foremost, social media has been linked to an increase in mental health issues, particularly among young people. The constant exposure to curated and manipulated content can create unrealistic expectations and promote consumerism, leading to feelings of inadequacy and low self-esteem. Furthermore, the anonymity of social media can facilitate cyberbullying, which can have severe consequences for the victims. According to a study by the Pew Research Center, 59% of teens have experienced online harassment, with 45% saying they have been subjected to severe forms of harassment.

In addition to its impact on mental health, social media has also been accused of promoting social comparison and decreasing face-to-face interaction. People often present a highlight reel of their lives on social media, showcasing their accomplishments and hiding their flaws. This can create a sense of competition and envy, as people compare their lives to the seemingly perfect ones presented online. As a result, people are spending more time interacting with their screens and less time engaging with the world around them. A study by the University of California, Irvine found that people who spent more time on social media were more likely to experience social isolation, even if they had a large number of friends.

Another significant concern is the spread of misinformation on social media. With the ease of creating and sharing content, false information can quickly go viral, often with serious consequences. For example, during the COVID-19 pandemic, social media platforms were awash with false information about the virus, its symptoms, and its treatments. This not only created confusion but also put people's lives at risk. According to a study by the Knight Foundation, 70% of adults in the US believe that fake news has a significant impact on the country's political discourse.

Finally, social media has been criticized for its role in the erosion of civil discourse. The anonymity of social media can embolden people to express extreme views, often without consequences. This can create a toxic online environment, where people are more likely to engage in personal attacks and insults rather than respectful debate. A study by the Brookings Institution found that social media has contributed to the polarization of American politics, with people increasingly sorting themselves into like-minded groups and avoiding opposing viewpoints.

In conclusion, while social media has its benefits, its negative effects cannot be ignored. The impact on mental health, social comparison, the spread of misinformation, and the erosion of civil discourse all contribute to a toxic online environment. It is essential that we take steps to mitigate these effects, such as promoting media literacy, encouraging respectful online behavior, and holding social media companies accountable for the content they host. Only by acknowledging the negative effects of social media can we work towards creating a healthier and more constructive online community.

In conclusion, climate change is a pressing issue that requires immediate attention and action. The topic of standardized testing has long been a subject of debate in the education sector. While proponents of standardized testing argue that it provides an objective measure of student performance, I firmly believe that it is a flawed system that does more harm than good.

Standardized tests, such as the SAT and ACT, have been a staple of the college admissions process for decades. However, these tests have been shown to be biased towards students from affluent backgrounds, who have greater access to test preparation resources. This creates an unfair advantage for students from wealthy families, who are able to afford expensive tutoring and test prep courses.

Moreover, standardized tests do not accurately reflect a student's intelligence or potential. They are limited in scope, focusing primarily on math and reading comprehension, and do not account for other important skills such as creativity, critical thinking, and problem-solving. This narrow focus can lead to a lack of diversity in the types of students who are accepted into top universities, as students who excel in other areas are often overlooked.

Additionally, the emphasis on standardized testing can have a negative impact on students' mental health and well-being. The high-stakes nature of these tests can create immense pressure and stress, leading to anxiety and burnout. This can have long-term consequences, affecting not only a student's academic performance but also their overall well-being.

In conclusion, while standardized testing may have been intended to provide a fair and objective measure of student performance, it has ultimately created a system that is biased, limited, and harmful to students. It is time to reevaluate our reliance on standardized testing and consider alternative methods of assessment that take into account a broader range of skills and abilities. By doing so, we can create a more inclusive and equitable education system that truly supports the diverse needs and talents of all students.

For one, UBI would provide a safety net for the most vulnerable members of society, such as the homeless and the disabled. It would also give people the financial security to pursue their passions and interests, rather than just taking any job for the sake of a paycheck.

Moreover, UBI would have a positive impact on the economy as a whole. It would put more money in people's pockets, which would increase consumer spending and boost economic growth. Additionally, UBI would reduce poverty and income inequality, which are major drivers of social unrest and crime. 

Some may argue that UBI would reduce the incentive to work, but I would counter that this is a misconception. Many people want to work and contribute to society, but are unable to do so due to circumstances beyond their control. UBI would give them the opportunity to pursue meaningful work and contribute to their communities.

In conclusion, while there are certainly challenges to implementing UBI, I firmly believe that it is a necessary step towards creating a more just and equitable society. It would provide a safety net for the most vulnerable, promote economic growth, and reduce poverty and income inequality. As such, I strongly advocate for the implementation of UBI and urge policymakers to take a closer look at this innovative solution.

The Impact of Social Media on Mental Health: A Growing Concern. 
Social media has become an integral part of our daily lives, with billions of people around the world using platforms like Instagram, Facebook, and Twitter. While social media has its benefits, such as connecting us with others and providing a platform for self-expression, it also has a darker side. Excessive social media use has been linked to a range of mental health problems, including anxiety, depression, and loneliness. 
One of the main reasons social media can be harmful to our mental health is the way it presents a curated version of other people's lives. We see the highlight reels of our friends' and celebrities' lives, and it's easy to compare and feel like we don't measure up. This can lead to feelings of inadequacy and low self-esteem, which can be particularly damaging for young people who are still developing their sense of identity.
Furthermore, social media can be addictive, activating the brain's reward system and releasing feel-good chemicals like dopamine. This can lead to a vicious cycle of constant checking and scrolling, as we become hooked on the instant gratification and validation that social media provides. 
However, it's not all doom and gloom. Social media can also be a powerful tool for good, providing a platform for people to connect with others who share similar experiences and interests. It can also be a useful resource for people who are struggling with mental health issues, providing access to support groups and online therapy sessions. 
In conclusion, while social media has its benefits, it's clear that excessive use can have a negative impact on our mental health. By being aware of the potential risks and taking steps to mitigate them, we can use social media in a way that promotes positive mental health and wellbeing. This can involve setting boundaries around our social media use, taking regular breaks, and engaging in offline activities that bring us joy and fulfillment.

This can lead to a lack of engagement and motivation among students, as they are forced to memorize and regurgitate information rather than explore and learn. This can have long-term effects on a student's mental health and self-esteem, as they may begin to view themselves as failures or inadequate. 

In contrast, many countries have adopted alternative approaches to assessment, such as competency-based progression and project-based evaluations, which allow students to demonstrate their knowledge and skills in a more holistic and meaningful way. These approaches prioritize student learning and understanding over test scores and grades, and have been shown to lead to improved academic outcomes and increased student engagement.

In conclusion, while standardized testing may provide some benefits, such as accountability and comparability, its limitations and drawbacks far outweigh its advantages. Student-designed Projects Encourage Learning

Summers can be boring for students, especially when homework is assigned. Students have creative minds and a variety of interests which can be specialized to a topic of interest; however, schools tend to assign a generic assignment to all students despite their differences. Summer projects are intended to enable students to continue learning and exploring the world through a lense of their interest. Therefore, allowing students to design their own summer projects allows for their interests to spark, their creativity to grow, and their areas of knowledge to expand.

Firstly, student-designed summer projects will allow for every student to specify the project on his or her interests. Every child is different and shows admiration towards different subjects in school. If teachers design the summer project, the students will lack incentive to explore an area of interest as that has already been done for them. Additionally, teachers will attempt to design the summer project in a way that it applies to all students; however, not all students think alike. For example, most middle schools conduct science fairs that allow kids to explore an area of science that particularly interests them. This allows for children to research heavily into a subject and even enjoy doing so. This not only sparks an interest for science, but it also allows students to show off their abilities and specialize in their talents. This science fair analogy can be applied to summer projects because children will develop their admiration towards an educational topic and will enjoy the learning process. This creates a positive incentive for learning despite it being summer.

Secondly, if students are enabled to design their own summer projects, creativity will occur and develop. When teachers design projects, students are incentified to simply follow instructions and do as they are told. This results in surface level researching and a lack of interest in actually learning and retaining knowledge. This is understandable as most students do not enjoy a generic assignment that does not apply specifically to their interests. However, if students were given the opportunity to design their own project, they could research a subject that sparks their interest and creativity. This will lead to a deeper understanding of the topic and will result in a better quality of summer projects completed over all. For example, refering back to the science fair analogy, most students will become creative and design their own experiments if they are given the opportunity to do so. Most students enjoy being given the freedom and trust to become creative and show off their interests.

Lastly, when students return to school after summer break, they will see a variety of interesting summer projects completed by their classmates. The student-designed projects allow for a large variety of topics to be explored, and will benefit the students intensely. If all students, for example, have the same assignment, they would be less interested in their classmates projects as they would all be generically similar. However, if the students have the opportunity to design and conduct their own research into their favorite topic, then the students can share each others interesting new insights with each other and spread their knowledge. This increases students admiration for learning and will inentify them to study something interesting for their classmates.

In conclusion, allowing students to design their own summer projects allows for their interests to be explored, their creativity to flourish, and their areas of knowledge to expand. Schools tend to fail to recognise that each student is different, and that he or she requires different learning styles in order to be successfull in learning. It is vital that students are given the opportunity to become creative and explore an interest that is dear to them. If this is not prioritized, schools will continue to foster the idea of simply following instructions.

I feel that working with a partner is more beneficial to students. Working with partners gets students extra help when in need. It can make new friends while working on big projects. Also it makes the work get done easier and quicker when working in big groups. I also personally think that any project with a presentation should be a group project. If that presentation has more than just the presentation it should be a three person group.

Working with a partner is beneficial to students, because it gives extra support or help on a project or classwork. If a project is too big and impossible for one person to complete they could split up the work. For example, when I had a final project in my english class; I separated the work with my partner. We had to do an essay and a PowerPoint presentation. My partner did the essay and did the PowerPoint presentation and we both finished in time. If I hadn't had my partner, I probably would not have finished the project in time. My teacher making it a group project made it way easier to do because I didn't have to worry about writing essay.

Another reason that working with partners is beneficial to students is that they can build new friendship while doing work. When students are doing work in groups, they are together the whole class and have to stay in contact outside of school. For example, when I was working on a video for my journalism class I had a very big video that was due in a few days. I made good friends with the people that were in that group because we spent the whole class together and staying in contact after school. Every time I'm making a video I want to work with them because I know they will do a good job.

Another way that working in partner benefits students is that it saves them time and makes them finish their work quicker. If the students split up their work and do their work efficiently they will finish quickly. The more group members will make it even quicker. For example, when I was working with a friend and two other students on a project for a book we finished the book very quickly and the book review was finished very quickly as well. When partners are helping each other it makes everything way easier and more fun as well, because you get to hang out with your friends while being productive.

Also if the teacher lets students pick people, they can pick people that know a lot about the topic of the project or classwork. For example, in when I had spanish we did a project about Puerto Rico and since I'm from Puerto Rico everyone wanted to pick me. I went to a group where a good friend of mine was and the project was very easy to finish and present. The project was done so quickly that the next class we had free time for the whole class. That's another reason why working in groups is so beneficial and good.

Working with partners can also make students more comfortable with the subject or the project. Students sometimes get handed a project or classwork without knowing what to do. Having a partner to help the out is great so they can get comfortable with the subject or the project. For example, when I was Earth and Space Science I had no idea what to do on a project the teacher was assigning. She assigned partners and my partner told me what to do and I finally understood. The project took us about two days to finish but it was a very hard project to do that would have been impossible to finish alone.

Groups of at least three people should be required for project of more than 2 assignments. Two people can't do a project with five assignments and should have that extra person to split up the work and no one does extra work. For example, when I was in the sixth grade I had a project where I had to write about Mozart's story and I had to write an two paragraphs, buy and design a poster board, and also give a presentation and memorize everything. I did the essay but forgot to do the poster board until the night before. I had to stay up to 12:30 at midnight doing the poster and memorizing the 2 paragraphs. If the teacher would have made it a group project, I wouldn't have had to worry about the poster because my group members were on top of it.

Another reason that groups of at least three people benefit students is that maybe one of the students doesn't want to do any work there's still another group member left that wants to do the work. For example, my english teacher gave us a presentation to do on PowerPoint and we split up the slides. But one of the group members didn't do anything, so the other group member and me had to do all of his work. We presented got points and he didn't. That's why it's so important to have groups of at least three people, because you still have a backup.
